s: On Mount Sinai God tells Moses that Israel will turn away and be scattered, then repent and be restored. He orders the angel of the presence to write down all history for Moses.
The angel tells of the six days of creation, including the creation of the angels on the first day, and of the Sabbath, which Israel alone is to keep.
Adam names the animals, and Eve is made from his rib. They live seven years in Eden, then sin and are driven out. The animals lose their speech.
Cain kills Abel. The family of Adam and the names of his daughters. Enoch is the first to learn writing and is taken into Eden. Adam dies.
The Watchers take human wives and father giants. God binds the angels and sends the flood, and Noah builds the ark.
Noah leaves the ark and offers sacrifice. God makes a covenant with him and the rainbow is its sign. The Feast of Weeks and the 364-day calendar are given.
Noah plants a vine and is shamed by Ham, and he curses Canaan. Noah warns his sons against blood and the ways of the Watchers.
Kainam finds the Watchers' teaching on the stars and sins. Noah divides the earth among his three sons by lot.
Shem, Ham and Japheth divide their portions among their sons.
Evil spirits lead Noah's grandchildren astray. At Noah's prayer nine tenths of them are bound, and one tenth is left to Mastema, their chief. Noah dies. The tower of Babel.
Idolatry spreads. Abram is born, and as a boy he drives away the ravens sent by Mastema to eat the seed.
Abram tells his father Terah that idols are nothing and burns the house of idols. He studies the stars, turns to God and is called to leave Haran.
Abram enters Canaan and goes down to Egypt. He separates from Lot and rescues him from the kings, and the law of tithes is given.
God makes a covenant with Abram between the pieces. Hagar bears Ishmael.
God changes Abram's name to Abraham and gives circumcision as an eternal law. The angels themselves are circumcised.
The angels visit Abraham. Sodom is destroyed. Isaac is born, and Abraham is the first to keep the Feast of Tabernacles.
Isaac is weaned, and Hagar and Ishmael are sent away. Mastema challenges God to test Abraham's faith.
Abraham is told to offer Isaac and obeys. The angel stops him, and the feast of the seven days is kept in memory.
Sarah dies and is buried. Isaac marries Rebecca. Jacob and Esau are born, and Abraham loves Jacob and blesses him.
Abraham calls his sons and grandsons and commands them to do justice and avoid idolatry and fornication.
Abraham teaches Isaac the laws of sacrifice and warns him against eating blood.
Abraham keeps the Feast of Weeks with his sons, blesses Jacob and commands him not to marry a daughter of Canaan. Then he lies down to die with Jacob in his arms.
Abraham dies and is buried. The angel tells how lives will grow shorter because of sin, and foretells the evils of the last days and a time of renewal.
Esau sells his birthright. Isaac goes to Gerar, digs wells, and makes a treaty with the Philistines.
Rebecca tells Jacob not to marry a Canaanite woman, and blesses him.
Jacob, helped by Rebecca, receives Isaac's blessing in place of Esau, who asks for a blessing of his own.
Rebecca sends Jacob away to Laban. On the way he dreams at Bethel of a ladder to heaven.
Jacob serves Laban and marries Leah and Rachel. His twelve children are born, and he grows rich.
Jacob leaves Laban, makes a covenant with him, and is reconciled with Esau.
Dinah is defiled at Shechem, and her brothers take revenge. The law against marrying foreigners. Levi is chosen for the priesthood.
Jacob goes up to Bethel with his household. Isaac blesses Levi for the priesthood and Judah for rule.
Levi is ordained priest and Jacob gives a tithe. Jacob is renamed Israel. The second tithe is to be eaten before God.
Reuben sins with Bilhah. The laws against incest. Jacob's twelve sons are listed.
Jacob and his sons defeat the Amorite kings. Joseph is sold, and Jacob mourns him on the day later kept as the Day of Atonement.
Rebecca asks Jacob and Esau to love each other, and makes them swear it. She dies.
Isaac blesses his sons and divides his goods between them, warning Esau not to harm Jacob. Isaac dies.
Esau's sons persuade him to break his oath and attack Jacob.
Jacob kills Esau in battle, and the sons of Esau are made subject to Jacob. The kings of Edom are listed.
Joseph in Potiphar's house resists his master's wife, is thrown into prison, and interprets the dreams of the butler and baker.
Joseph interprets Pharaoh's dreams and is made ruler over Egypt.
Judah and Tamar. Judah repents and is forgiven, and the law on this sin is given.
The famine comes. Joseph's brothers come to Egypt for grain, and Joseph keeps Simeon.
Joseph tests his brothers with the cup, then reveals himself and forgives them.
Jacob keeps the Feast of Weeks, and goes down to Egypt with his family, seventy souls.
Jacob meets Joseph and settles in Goshen. Jacob dies and is buried in Canaan.
Joseph dies. A new king oppresses Israel and orders the boys to be killed.
Moses is born, saved from the river and raised by Pharaoh's daughter. He kills an Egyptian and flees to Midian.
Moses is sent back to Egypt. Mastema tries to kill him and helps the Egyptians, but God's angels defend Israel and drown the Egyptians in the sea.
The laws of the Passover, to be kept on the fourteenth day of the first month and eaten within the courts of the sanctuary.
The laws of the jubilees and of the Sabbath. Israel will be free in its land when the jubilees are complete.
i: Jubilees retells Genesis and the first part of Exodus, from the Creation to the giving of the Law on Sinai, as a revelation that an angel dictated to Moses on the mountain. It was written in Hebrew by a Jewish priestly author in the second century before Christ; fragments of at least fourteen copies were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Only the Ethiopian Church kept the whole book, and she reads it as Scripture.

Its name comes from its timeline: all of history is counted in “jubilees”, periods of 49 years, and every event is dated by them. The author defends a calendar of 364 days, so that the feasts always fall on the same day of the week, and he shows the patriarchs already keeping the Sabbath, the feasts and the laws of purity long before Moses.

What to expect: much will be familiar from Genesis, with added stories, for example the names of Adam’s daughters, Abraham as a boy breaking his father’s idols, and long blessings and farewell speeches. The Catholic Church does not count it among the books of the Bible.
